newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam lays down law on tobacco, alcohol adverts.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam lays down law on tobacco, alcohol adverts.

text.p: Vietnam said on Tuesday it had reissued directives for a total ban on the advertising of cigarettes and most alcohol, amid an accelerating government austerity drive.
An official at the Culture and Information Ministry said the measure was aimed at reinforcing previously existing regulations which, she said, were routinely flouted.
The ban covers all forms of liquor and cigarette advertising and sets new limits on the number of media advertisements for beer.
"Recently people have taken advantage of the Tet (lunar new year) festival to get round the rules by placing seasonal greetings with their brand names in local newspapers," she said.
"This is a kind of advertising, and we're aiming to stop it."

This year's Tet festival falls in early February. The period ahead of the holiday is one of the busiest of the year for the retail consumer market, a fact usually reflected by a sharp seasonal spike on inflation graphs.
Government efforts to tackle the problem this year, however, have coincided with wider moves aimed at tackling consumerism in one of Asia's remaining communist states through enforced thrift.
An editorial in Tuesday's party newspaper, the Nhan Dan, said wasteful and unnecessary spending should be strictly criticised and prevented both through education programmes and by law.

The newspaper, Vietnam's leading official daily, said regulations governing the spending of state funds on luxury goods and entertaining should be tightened, while popular consumerism should be strictly discouraged.

Advertisers and beer companies declined comment on the Culture Ministry announcement, but an official at the state-owned Thang Long Tobacco Company told Reuters he believed the impact would be limited.
"We feel quite unhappy with this," he said. "We contribute to the state budget and we've even won a labour award for excellence... but I don't expect this to make much difference."
